claim: TAF9B is selectively up-regulated upon in vitro motor neuron differentiation.
source: Here, we report that the orphan TBP-associated factor TAF9B is selectively up-regulated upon in vitro motor neuron differentiation
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR and Western blot data showing increased TAF9B expression during motor neuron differentiation (Figure 1C, 1D).

claim: TAF9B is required for the transcriptional induction of specific neuronal genes.
source: Here, we report that the orphan TBP-associated factor TAF9B is selectively up-regulated upon in vitro motor neuron differentiation, and is required for the transcriptional induction of specific neuronal genes
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq analysis showing down-regulation of neuronal genes in Taf9b KO cells (Figure 4).

claim: TAF9B is dispensable for global gene expression in murine ES cells.
source: Here, we report that the orphan TBP-associated factor TAF9B is selectively up-regulated upon in vitro motor neuron differentiation, and is required for the transcriptional induction of specific neuronal genes, while dispensable for global gene expression in murine ES cells.
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq analysis showing only a small number of genes deregulated in Taf9b KO ES cells (Figure 2E).

claim: TAF9B binds to both promoters and distal enhancers of neuronal genes.
source: TAF9B binds to both promoters and distal enhancers of neuronal genes
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq data showing TAF9B binding at TSS and distal regions (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 1B, 1C).

claim: TAF9B partially co-localizes at binding sites of OLIG2.
source: TAF9B binds to both promoters and distal enhancers of neuronal genes, partially co-localizing at binding sites of OLIG2, a key activator of motor neuron differentiation.
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq analysis showing overlap between TAF9B and OLIG2 binding sites (Figure 5C).

claim: OLIG2 is a key activator of motor neuron differentiation.
source: TAF9B binds to both promoters and distal enhancers of neuronal genes, partially co-localizing at binding sites of OLIG2, a key activator of motor neuron differentiation.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the context of the manuscript.

claim: In the neuronal context, TAF9B becomes preferentially associated with PCAF rather than the canonical TFIID complex.
source: Surprisingly, in this neuronal context TAF9B becomes preferentially associated with PCAF rather than the canonical TFIID complex.
evidence: Supported by co-immunoprecipitation experiments showing TAF9B association with PCAF but not with TFIID components TAF4 and TAF7 (Figure 6A, 6C).

claim: TAF9B regulates neuronal gene transcription in vivo in dissected spinal column from Taf9b KO mice.
source: Analysis of dissected spinal column from Taf9b KO mice confirmed that TAF9B also regulates neuronal gene transcription in vivo.
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq analysis of spinal column tissue showing down-regulation of neuronal genes in Taf9b KO mice (Figure 7C, 7D, 7E).

claim: Alternative core promoter complexes may provide a key mechanism to lock in and maintain specific transcriptional programs in terminally differentiated cell types.
source: Our findings suggest that alternative core promoter complexes may provide a key mechanism to lock in and maintain specific transcriptional programs in terminally differentiated cell types.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the findings about TAF9B function.

claim: Sequence-specific transcription factors are essential for directing cellular differentiation and identity.
source: Sequence-specific transcription factors are essential for directing cellular differentiation and identity.
evidence: This is stated as established scientific knowledge.

claim: Sequence-specific transcription factors play key roles in establishing gene expression patterns that dictate cell-type specific functions and characteristics.
source: These factors play key roles in establishing gene expression patterns that dictate cell-type specific functions and characteristics.
evidence: This is stated as established scientific knowledge.

claim: Targeted expression of particular sets of transcription factors can control cell fate.
source: Cellular reprogramming and de-differentiation leading to the formation of induced pluripotent stem cells offer dramatic examples of how targeted expression of particular sets of transcription factors can control cell fate (reviewed by Graf, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Graf, 2011.

claim: Core promoter factors have traditionally been considered invariant and universally required for the expression of all protein-coding genes.
source: These core promoter factors often called 'basal' or 'general' transcription factors have traditionally been considered invariant and universally required for the expression of all protein-coding genes.
evidence: This is stated as historical scientific understanding.

claim: Some components of the pre-initiation complex can exhibit both promoter and enhancer targeting activities that are cell-type specific.
source: However, recent studies suggest that at least some components of this large and diverse group of factors necessary to form the transcriptional pre-initiation complex (PIC) can exhibit both promoter and enhancer targeting activities that are cell-type specific. This specificity depends on the variegated composition of the components in the PIC (reviewed in D'Alessio et al., 2009; Goodrich and Tjian, 2010; Müller et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to D'Alessio et al., 2009; Goodrich and Tjian, 2010; Müller et al., 2010.

claim: TAF4B controls oocyte-specific activation of transcription in mouse ovaries.
source: A paralog of TAF4, called TAF4B, was found to control oocyte-specific activation of transcription in mouse ovaries (Freiman et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Freiman et al., 2001.

claim: In Drosophila, five TAF paralogs (No hitter/TAF4; Cannonball/TAF5; Meiois I arrest/TAF6; Spermatocyte arrest/TAF8; and Ryan express/TAF12) all play specific roles in spermatogenesis.
source: In Drosophila, a group of five TAF paralogs (No hitter/TAF4; Cannonball/TAF5; Meiois I arrest/TAF6; Spermatocyte arrest/TAF8; and Ryan express/TAF12) all play specific roles in spermatogenesis (Hiller et al., 2004; Chen et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hiller et al., 2004; Chen et al., 2005.

claim: TAF7L cooperates with TRF2 to regulate spermatogenesis in mice.
source: Similarly, another orphan TAF, TAF7L, cooperates with TBP-related factor 2 (TRF2) to regulate spermatogenesis in mice (Cheng et al., 2007; Zhou et al., 2013a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Cheng et al., 2007; Zhou et al., 2013a.

claim: TAF7L acts in conjunction with PPARγ to control the transcription necessary for adipogenesis in adipocytes.
source: Tissue-specific functions of TAF7L were also found in adipocytes where it acts in conjunction with PPARγ to control the transcription necessary for adipogenesis (Zhou et al., 2013b).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Zhou et al., 2013b.

claim: In mouse embryonic stem cells, TAF3 pairs up with CTCF to drive the expression of endoderm specific genes.
source: In mouse embryonic stem (ES) cells, TAF3 pairs up with CTCF to drive the expression of endoderm specific genes while in myoblasts TAF3 works with TRF3 in the differentiation of myotubes (Deato and Tjian, 2007; Liu et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Deato and Tjian, 2007; Liu et al., 2011.

claim: In myoblasts, TAF3 works with TRF3 in the differentiation of myotubes.
source: In mouse embryonic stem (ES) cells, TAF3 pairs up with CTCF to drive the expression of endoderm specific genes while in myoblasts TAF3 works with TRF3 in the differentiation of myotubes (Deato and Tjian, 2007; Liu et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Deato and Tjian, 2007; Liu et al., 2011.

claim: Loss of motor neurons gives rise to devastating diseases, including amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS).
source: Loss of motor neurons gives rise to devastating diseases, including amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) (reviewed by Robberecht and Philips, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Robberecht and Philips, 2013.

claim: Several key classical sequence-specific DNA-binding transcription factors regulating the expression of motor neuron-specific genes have been identified.
source: Consequently, motor neurons have been the focus of intense study and several key classical sequence-specific DNA-binding transcription factors regulating the expression of motor neuron-specific genes have been identified (reviewed by di Sanguinetto et al., 2008; Kanning et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to di Sanguinetto et al., 2008; Kanning et al., 2010.

claim: Taf9b was significantly up-regulated in GFP expressing (GFP+) motor neurons but not in the GFP negative (GFP−) cells.
source: Intriguingly, one TAF paralog (Taf9b) was significantly up-regulated in GFP expressing (GFP+) motor neurons but not in the GFP negative (GFP−) cells (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The up-regulation of TAF9B and down-regulation of several other TAFs occur at the level of both mRNA and protein.
source: We confirmed that the up-regulation of TAF9B and down-regulation of several other TAFs occur at the level of both mRNA and protein (Figure 1D)
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: TAF9B expression follows the kinetics of post-mitotic neuronal marker Tubb3 but not the progenitor cell markers Pax6 and Olig2.
source: We confirmed that the up-regulation of TAF9B and down-regulation of several other TAFs occur at the level of both mRNA and protein (Figure 1D), and follows the kinetics of post-mitotic neuronal marker Tubb3 but not the progenitor cell markers Pax6 and Olig2 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Most Taf subunits of TFIID in newborn spinal cord are expressed at lower levels than in mouse ES cells.
source: As expected, most Taf subunits of TFIID in newborn spinal cord are expressed at lower levels than in mouse ES cells, while Taf9b is up-regulated more than 10-fold, consistent with the results obtained with the in vitro differentiated motor neurons (Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Taf9b is up-regulated more than 10-fold in newborn spinal cord compared to mouse ES cells.
source: As expected, most Taf subunits of TFIID in newborn spinal cord are expressed at lower levels than in mouse ES cells, while Taf9b is up-regulated more than 10-fold, consistent with the results obtained with the in vitro differentiated motor neurons (Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Many components of the PIC and selected co-activators were down-regulated upon neuronal differentiation.
source: We also found that many components of the PIC and selected co-activators were down-regulated upon neuronal differentiation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D and 1E).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D and 1E.

claim: Induction of TAF9B upon neuronal differentiation is specific and distinct from regulated expression of most other subunits of the PIC.
source: These results strongly suggest that induction of TAF9B upon neuronal differentiation is specific and distinct from regulated expression of most other subunits of the PIC.
evidence: This is an inference based on the differential expression patterns observed.

claim: In Taf9b KO ES cells, all protein-coding exons of Taf9b have been replaced with the LacZ-Neo cassette.
source: In these cells, all protein-coding exons of Taf9b have been replaced with the LacZ-Neo cassette (Figure 2A).
evidence: This describes the genetic modification made to generate the KO cells.

claim: The induction of Taf9b upon motor neuron differentiation was detected only in wild type (WT) cells but not in Taf9b KO cells.
source: As expected, the induction of Taf9b upon motor neuron differentiation was detected only in wild type (WT) cells but not in Taf9b KO cells (Figure 2B,C).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR and Western blot data shown in Figure 2B and 2C.

claim: Taf9b KO cells have a normal mouse ES cell morphology.
source: We found that Taf9b KO cells have a normal mouse ES cell morphology and can be grown in the presence of LIF without displaying any obvious cell growth or cell cycle defects (Figure 2D and data not shown).
evidence: This is based on morphological observation and cell cycle analysis shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Taf9b KO cells can be grown in the presence of LIF without displaying any obvious cell growth or cell cycle defects.
source: We found that Taf9b KO cells have a normal mouse ES cell morphology and can be grown in the presence of LIF without displaying any obvious cell growth or cell cycle defects (Figure 2D and data not shown).
evidence: Supported by cell cycle analysis shown in Figure 2D.

claim: TAF9B is largely dispensable for global gene expression in murine ES cells with only a small number of genes deregulated.
source: The results show that TAF9B is largely dispensable for global gene expression with only a small number of genes deregulated under these conditions (Figure 2E).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Core TAF components of TFIID are critical for murine ES cell pluripotency and in controlling genes such as Pou5f1, Nanog and Klf4.
source: Interestingly, whereas the core TAF components of TFIID have recently been reported to be critical for murine ES cell pluripotency and in controlling genes such as Pou5f1, Nanog and Klf4 (Pijnappel et al., 2013), the absence of TAF9B did not affect expression of pluripotency markers (Figure 2E,F).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Pijnappel et al., 2013.

claim: The absence of TAF9B did not affect expression of pluripotency markers.
source: Interestingly, whereas the core TAF components of TFIID have recently been reported to be critical for murine ES cell pluripotency and in controlling genes such as Pou5f1, Nanog and Klf4 (Pijnappel et al., 2013), the absence of TAF9B did not affect expression of pluripotency markers (Figure 2E,F).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq and qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 2E and 2F.

claim: Unlike other TAFs present in the canonical TFIID complex, TAF9B is dispensable for global gene expression and pluripotency of murine ES cells.
source: These results suggest that, unlike other TAFs present in the canonical TFIID complex, TAF9B is dispensable for global gene expression and pluripotency of murine ES cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the RNA-seq and qRT-PCR data.

claim: A significant reduction in motor neuron markers Isl1, Mnx1, and Lhx3 was observed in Taf9b KO cells upon differentiation.
source: We observed a significant reduction in all motor neuron markers in Taf9b KO cells upon differentiation (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Motor neuron differentiation was compromised in Taf9b KO cells as confirmed by immunostaining for ISL1/2 and western blot for TUBB3.
source: Immunostaining for motor neuron marker ISL1/2 as well as western blot analysis for TUBB3 further confirmed that motor neuron differentiation was compromised in Taf9b KO cells (Figure 3B,C).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining and Western blot data shown in Figure 3B and 3C.

claim: Taf9b KO cells failed to efficiently down-regulate ES cell markers Pou5f1 and Nanog upon differentiation.
source: We next measured the down-regulation of ES specific markers Pou5f1 and Nanog upon differentiation and found that Taf9b KO cells failed to efficiently down-regulate these ES cell markers (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: A fraction of cells in neuralized EBs derived from Taf9b KO cells continue to express pluripotency markers OCT4 and NANOG, whereas few or no cells expressing OCT4 and NANOG were detected in WT cells.
source: Immunostaining of OCT4 and NANOG confirmed that a fraction of cells in these neuralized EBs derived from Taf9b KO cells continue to express pluripotency markers, whereas few or no cells expressing OCT4 and NANOG were detected in WT cells (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: A higher number of dividing cells persisted in Taf9b KO EBs as determined by the marker for cellular proliferation Ki67.
source: Consistent with the maintenance of an undifferentiated state, a higher number of dividing cells persisted in Taf9b KO EBs as determined by the marker for cellular proliferation Ki67 (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: An increase in apoptosis was found in Taf9b KO cells compared to WT controls during early stages of differentiation.
source: We also found an increase in apoptosis in Taf9b KO cells compared to WT controls during early stages of differentiation (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by apoptosis assay data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Differences in apoptosis were particularly prominent at day 4 when progenitor cells are most enriched.
source: These differences in apoptosis were particularly prominent at day 4 when progenitor cells are most enriched.
evidence: This is based on the apoptosis assay data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: TAF9B has been implicated in cell survival and control of apoptosis in human HeLa cells.
source: This is consistent with previous observations implicating TAF9B in cell survival and control of apoptosis in human HeLa cells (Chen and Manley, 2003; Frontini et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Chen and Manley, 2003; Frontini et al., 2005.

claim: TAF9B is required for the efficient in vitro differentiation of murine ES cells into motor neurons.
source: Taken in aggregate, our findings suggest that TAF9B is required for the efficient in vitro differentiation of murine ES cells into motor neurons
evidence: This is an inference based on the differentiation defects observed in Taf9b KO cells.

claim: The absence of TAF9B causes the persistent expression of pluripotency markers under differentiation conditions.
source: Taken in aggregate, our findings suggest that TAF9B is required for the efficient in vitro differentiation of murine ES cells into motor neurons, and that the absence of TAF9B causes the persistent expression of pluripotency markers under differentiation conditions.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of continued OCT4 and NANOG expression in Taf9b KO cells during differentiation.

claim: As motor neuron differentiation progressed there was a concomitant increase in the number of genes deregulated by the loss of TAF9B.
source: We found that as motor neuron differentiation progressed there was a concomitant increase in the number of genes deregulated by the loss of TAF9B (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Striking deregulation of genes in Taf9b KO cells was observed at day 4 when progenitor cells are most enriched in these cultures.
source: Striking deregulation of genes in Taf9b KO cells was observed at the time point at which progenitor cells are most enriched in these cultures (day 4).
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq data analysis.

claim: Genes important for neuronal progenitor identity such as Olig2, Pax6, Sox1, Nkx6-1, Nkx6-2, Gli1, and genes controlled by the Notch signaling pathway were among the most down-regulated by the loss of TAF9B.
source: Genes known to be important for neuronal progenitor identity such as Olig2, Pax6, Sox1, Nkx6-1, Nkx6-2, Gli1, and genes controlled by the Notch signaling pathway were among the most down-regulated by the loss of TAF9B (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Gene ontology terms analysis of down-regulated genes showed categories such as neuron differentiation and anterior/posterior pattern formation among the most enriched terms.
source: Gene ontology (GO) terms analysis of down-regulated genes showed categories such as neuron differentiation and anterior/posterior pattern formation among the most enriched terms (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by GO term analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Among up-regulated genes in Taf9b KO cells at day 4 were genes involved in apoptosis.
source: Among up-regulated genes we found genes involved in apoptosis (Supplementary file 1), which is consistent with the increase in apoptosis levels we observed in Taf9b KO cells at this time point.
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data in Supplementary file 1.

claim: By day 6, approximately 10% of all expressed genes were down-regulated and another 10% were up-regulated in Taf9b KO cells.
source: By day 6, when post-mitotic motor neurons are normally present in these cultures, approximately 10% of all expressed genes were down-regulated and another 10% were up-regulated in Taf9b KO cells.
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq data analysis.

claim: TAF9B is specifically required for the appropriate expression of a subset of genes, rather than for global gene expression in differentiated EBs.
source: This finding suggests that TAF9B is specifically required for the appropriate expression of a subset of genes, rather than for global gene expression in these differentiated EBs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the RNA-seq data showing selective gene deregulation.

claim: The most significant GO term categories of genes down-regulated by the loss of TAF9B at day 6 included genes involved in neuron differentiation, axogenesis, and neuron projection.
source: The most significant GO term categories of genes down-regulated by the loss of TAF9B in this time point included genes involved in neuron differentiation, axogenesis, and neuron projection (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by GO term analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Specific motor neuron markers Lhx3, Lhx4, Isl1, Mnx1, and pan-neuronal marker Tubb3 were among the most down-regulated genes in Taf9b KO cells at day 6.
source: Moreover, the specific motor neuron markers Lhx3, Lhx4, Isl1, Mnx1, and pan-neuronal marker Tubb3 were among the most down-regulated genes in Taf9b KO cells (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Genes up-regulated in Taf9b KO cells at day 6 were enriched in categories such as vascular development, stem cell maintenance, and other non-neuronal developmental categories.
source: In contrast, genes up-regulated in Taf9b KO cells were enriched in categories such as vascular development, stem cell maintenance, and other non-neuronal developmental categories (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by GO term analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Samples differentiated for 2 days have a relatively small number of genes affected in Taf9b KO cells.
source: Contrary to the large number of genes deregulated in neuralized EB samples, we found that samples differentiated for 2 days have a relatively small number of genes affected in Taf9b KO cells.
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq data analysis.

claim: Genes involved in differentiation were found among early down-regulated genes at day 2 in Taf9b KO cells.
source: Interestingly, genes involved in differentiation were still found among these early down-regulated genes (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data in Supplementary file 1.

claim: TAF9B controls the expression of specific genes required for the in vitro differentiation of murine ES cells into motor neurons.
source: These results indicate that TAF9B controls the expression of specific genes required at least for the in vitro differentiation of murine ES cells into motor neurons.
evidence: This is an inference based on the RNA-seq data showing gene deregulation during differentiation.

claim: Approximately a third of all detected TAF9B binding regions overlapped with RNA POL2 occupancy (TAF9B-POL2) and mapped generally near transcription start sites (TSS) of protein coding genes.
source: Approximately a third of all detected TAF9B binding regions overlapped with RNA POL2 occupancy (TAF9B-POL2) and mapped generally near transcription start sites (TSS) of protein coding genes (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B, 1C.

claim: TAF9B peaks located at TSS were not enriched at promoters of neuronal specific genes.
source: However, TAF9B peaks located at TSS were not enriched at promoters of neuronal specific genes (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by GO term analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Approximately two thirds of all TAF9B binding regions showed little or no overlap with regions of high RNA POL2 occupancy (TAF9B-only) and were generally located distal to annotated TSS.
source: Intriguingly, approximately two thirds of all TAF9B binding regions showed little or no overlap with regions of high RNA POL2 occupancy (TAF9B-only) and were generally located distal to annotated TSS (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 1B, 1C).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B, 1C.

claim: Genes with TAF9B bound to regions distal to their TSS were significantly enriched in neuronal genes categories, including GO terms such as midbrain-hindbrain boundary development, rostrocaudal neural tube patterning and dorsal spinal cord development.
source: Importantly, genes with TAF9B bound to regions distal to their TSS were significantly enriched in neuronal genes categories, including GO terms such as midbrain-hindbrain boundary development, rostrocaudal neural tube patterning and dorsal spinal cord development (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by GO term analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Several of the most down-regulated genes in the absence of TAF9B detected by RNA-seq (e.g., Neurog2 and Lhx4) were associated with TAF9B distal binding sites.
source: Several of the most down-regulated genes in the absence of TAF9B detected by RNA-seq (e.g., Neurog2 and Lhx4) were associated with TAF9B distal binding sites (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,E).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and 1E.

claim: Genes bearing distal TAF9B peaks (e.g., 500–5000 bp from TSS) showed a higher percentage of genes down-regulated in Taf9b KO neuralized EBs than control gene sets.
source: Moreover, genes bearing distal TAF9B peaks (e.g., 500–5000 bp from TSS) showed a higher percentage of genes down-regulated in Taf9b KO neuralized EBs than control gene sets (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Distal TAF9B binding sites are likely functional regulatory elements controlling neuronal genes.
source: Collectively, these results suggest that distal TAF9B binding sites are likely functional regulatory elements controlling neuronal genes.
evidence: This is an inference based on the ChIP-seq and RNA-seq data.

claim: Co-localization between TAF9B and OLIG2 was found at both the TAF9B distal peaks and at the TAF9B TSS peaks.
source: We found co-localization between TAF9B and OLIG2 at both the TAF9B distal peaks and at the TAF9B TSS peaks, suggesting that TAF9B and OLIG2 act in concert at a subset of neuronal genes to regulate gene expression during motor neuron development (Figure 5C).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: TAF9B and OLIG2 act in concert at a subset of neuronal genes to regulate gene expression during motor neuron development.
source: We found co-localization between TAF9B and OLIG2 at both the TAF9B distal peaks and at the TAF9B TSS peaks, suggesting that TAF9B and OLIG2 act in concert at a subset of neuronal genes to regulate gene expression during motor neuron development (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is an inference based on the co-localization data.

claim: The incomplete overlap of TAF9B and OLIG2 peaks may in part represent intrinsic differences between progenitor cells and post-mitotic neurons.
source: The incomplete overlap of TAF9B and OLIG2 peaks may in part represent intrinsic differences between progenitor cells and post-mitotic neurons, since the OLIG2 binding was performed with neuralized EBs enriched for progenitor cells while TAF9B mapping was done with EBs enriched for post-mitotic motor neurons.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the incomplete overlap.

claim: It is likely that TAF9B co-localizes with activators other than OLIG2 in the motor neuron developmental pathway.
source: In addition, it is likely that TAF9B co-localizes with activators other than OLIG2 in this developmental pathway.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the incomplete overlap with OLIG2.

claim: Little detectable association of TAF9B with TAF4 and TAF7, core components of the TFIID complex, was observed in in vitro differentiated motor neurons.
source: We observed little detectable association of TAF9B with TAF4 and TAF7, core components of the TFIID complex, while TBP antibodies co-IP'ed those TFIID components efficiently.
evidence: Supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: TBP antibodies co-immunoprecipitated TAF4 and TAF7 efficiently.
source: We observed little detectable association of TAF9B with TAF4 and TAF7, core components of the TFIID complex, while TBP antibodies co-IP'ed those TFIID components efficiently.
evidence: Supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: An association between TAF9B and PCAF was observed in in vitro differentiated motor neurons.
source: In contrast, we observed an association between TAF9B and PCAF, a histone acetyltransferase present in the mammalian SAGA complex (Figure 6A).
evidence: Supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: PCAF is a histone acetyltransferase present in the mammalian SAGA complex.
source: In contrast, we observed an association between TAF9B and PCAF, a histone acetyltransferase present in the mammalian SAGA complex (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: Immunoprecipitations of 293T cells transfected with flag-tagged versions of TAF9B or TAF9 confirmed that the IPs are specific for TAF9B and not the closely related TAF9 subunit.
source: Immunoprecipitations of 293T cells transfected with flag-tagged versions of TAF9B or TAF9 confirmed that these IPs are specific for TAF9B and not the closely related TAF9 subunit (Figure 6B).
evidence: Supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The interactions between TAF9B and PCAF occur in vivo in dissected spinal column tissue samples from WT and Taf9b KO newborn mice.
source: We also performed TAF9B co-IP experiments on dissected spinal column tissue samples from WT and Taf9b KO newborn mice, confirming that the interactions between TAF9B and PCAF occur in vivo (Figure 6C).
evidence: Supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: TAF9B primarily associates with PCAF likely in a SAGA-like complex rather than the canonical TFIID in murine neurons.
source: Thus, TAF9B primarily associates with PCAF likely in a SAGA-like complex rather than the canonical TFIID in murine neurons.
evidence: This is an inference based on the co-immunoprecipitation data.

claim: Taf9b KO mice are viable and fertile.
source: Taf9b KO mice were viable and fertile, though the number of pups and birth weights were reduced in Taf9b KO matings compared to WT controls (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is based on observation of the generated mice.

claim: The number of pups and birth weights were reduced in Taf9b KO matings compared to WT controls.
source: Taf9b KO mice were viable and fertile, though the number of pups and birth weights were reduced in Taf9b KO matings compared to WT controls (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Spinal cord isolated from newborn KO animals did not express TAF9B.
source: As expected, spinal cord isolated from newborn KO animals did not express TAF9B (Figure 7A,B, Figure 7—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by Western blot and qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 7A, 7B, and Figure 7—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Loss of TAF9B in vivo may affect not only motor neuron formation but perhaps also proper differentiation of other cell types present in the spinal cord.
source: Given that Taf9b KO cells in vitro showed clear de-regulation of genes in both progenitor cells and post-mitotic motor neurons (Figure 4), we surmised that loss of TAF9B in vivo may affect not only motor neuron formation but perhaps also proper differentiation of other cell types present in the spinal cord.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the in vitro data.

claim: Genes down-regulated in the absence of TAF9B in vivo are enriched for neuronal genes including gene categories such as neuron projection, synapse and axonogenesis.
source: Our data indicate that genes down-regulated in the absence of TAF9B are enriched for neuronal genes including gene categories such as neuron projection, synapse and axonogenesis (Figure 7D).
evidence: Supported by GO term analysis shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Among the down-regulated genes identified by RNA-seq in vivo were neuronal genes such as Map1b, L1cam, Nefm, Nefh, and Isl2.
source: Among the down-regulated genes identified by RNA-seq were neuronal genes such as Map1b, L1cam, Nefm, Nefh, and Isl2.
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq data analysis.

claim: Gene expression analysis by qRT-PCR of lumbar spinal column tissues confirmed that neuronal genes are consistently down-regulated in KO compared to WT littermate controls.
source: Gene expression analysis by qRT-PCR of lumbar spinal column tissues confirmed that those neuronal genes are consistently down-regulated in KO compared to WT littermate controls (Figure 7E).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: Several different markers of specific neuronal populations, as well as the general marker Tubb3, were affected in the absence of TAF9B.
source: Several different markers of specific neuronal populations, as well as the general marker Tubb3, were also affected in the absence of TAF9B, suggesting a global defect in neuronal gene expression in the spinal cord (Figure 7—figure supplement 1E; Supplementary file 2).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1E and Supplementary file 2.

claim: The absence of TAF9B suggests a global defect in neuronal gene expression in the spinal cord.
source: Several different markers of specific neuronal populations, as well as the general marker Tubb3, were also affected in the absence of TAF9B, suggesting a global defect in neuronal gene expression in the spinal cord (Figure 7—figure supplement 1E; Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is an inference based on the qRT-PCR data.

claim: The observed pan-neuronal down-regulation and loss of neuronal tissue may be due to problems in the control of gene expression that coordinates the precise differentiation of progenitor cells during neuronal development.
source: Our data suggest that the observed pan-neuronal down-regulation and loss of neuronal tissue may be due to problems in the control of gene expression that coordinates the precise differentiation of progenitor cells during neuronal development.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the data.

claim: TAF9B is specifically required for the regulation of neuronal genes during neuronal development in the spinal cord.
source: These in vivo results taken together with our in vitro differentiation studies strongly support the notion that TAF9B is specifically required for the regulation of neuronal genes during neuronal development in the spinal cord.
evidence: This is an inference based on both in vitro and in vivo data.

claim: Changes in core promoter complexes are integral to the transcriptional program leading to terminal differentiation.
source: Our results and those of several other studies probing tissue-specific activities of core promoter factors and co-activators suggest a model in which changes in these complexes are integral to the transcriptional program leading to terminal differentiation.
evidence: This is a speculative model based on the findings and cited literature.

claim: Core promoter complexes themselves must undergo compositional changes using cell type-specific components such as TAF9B.
source: We speculate that rather than existing as a static complex awaiting recruitment by these transcription factors, core promoter complexes themselves must undergo compositional changes using cell type-specific components such as TAF9B.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings.

claim: Alternative promoter complexes expand the diversity and number of possible protein–protein transactions necessary to achieve proper fine-tuned control of gene expression.
source: These alternative promoter complexes expand the diversity and number of possible protein–protein transactions necessary to achieve proper fine-tuned control of gene expression.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings.

claim: Diversified core machineries might provide a mechanism to help lock down and maintain the functions and identity of differentiated cell types.
source: Furthermore, we speculate that such diversified core machineries might provide a mechanism to help lock down and maintain the functions and identity of differentiated cell types.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings.

claim: Taf9 is highly expressed in both mouse ES cells and neurons.
source: We established that indeed Taf9 is highly expressed in both mouse ES cells and neurons (as detected by RNA-seq).
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq data analysis.

claim: It is possible that TAF9 partially compensates for the loss of TAF9B thus blunting further global gene expression defects in Taf9b KO cells.
source: It is possible that TAF9 partially compensates for the loss of TAF9B thus blunting further global gene expression defects in Taf9b KO cells.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed phenotype.

claim: In human HeLa and chicken DT40 cells partially redundant functions have been observed for TAF9B and TAF9 paralogs.
source: In human HeLa and chicken DT40 cells partially redundant functions have been observed for these paralogs (Chen and Manley, 2003; Frontini et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Chen and Manley, 2003; Frontini et al., 2005.

claim: Taf4b and Taf7l KO mice are viable but infertile.
source: Taf4b and Taf7l KO mice are also viable, but unlike Taf9b KO mice, they are infertile (Freiman et al., 2001; Falender, 2005; Zhou et al., 2013a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Freiman et al., 2001; Falender, 2005; Zhou et al., 2013a.

claim: TAF9B is not critical for gametogenesis, in contrast to TAF4B and TAF7L.
source: Our results suggest that TAF9B is not critical for gametogenesis, in contrast to what has been observed for these two other orphan TAFs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the viability and fertility of Taf9b KO mice.

claim: TAF9B is involved in the activation of neuronal genes by binding to distal and promoter proximal DNA regulatory elements associated with the histone acetyltransferase PCAF.
source: Instead, our results point to a model where TAF9B is involved in the activation of neuronal genes by binding to distal and promoter proximal DNA regulatory elements associated with the histone acetyltransferase PCAF that, like its paralog GCN5, are subunits of the SAGA/STAGA/TFTC complex.
evidence: This is an inference based on the ChIP-seq and co-IP data.

claim: PCAF, like its paralog GCN5, is a subunit of the SAGA/STAGA/TFTC complex.
source: Instead, our results point to a model where TAF9B is involved in the activation of neuronal genes by binding to distal and promoter proximal DNA regulatory elements associated with the histone acetyltransferase PCAF that, like its paralog GCN5, are subunits of the SAGA/STAGA/TFTC complex.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: The SAGA complex contains several TAFs shared with TFIID including TAF6, TAF9, TAF5, TAF10, TAF12, and a de-ubiquitinase (DUB) module that removes ubiquitin from histone H2B.
source: This complex contains several TAFs shared with TFIID including TAF6, TAF9, TAF5, TAF10, TAF12, and a de-ubiquitinase (DUB) module that removes ubiquitin from histone H2B (reviewed by Spedale et al., 2012; Weake and Workman, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Spedale et al., 2012; Weake and Workman, 2012.

claim: It is possible that TAF9B is affecting the competitive recruitment or activity of a SAGA-like complex in place of TFIID.
source: Because TAFs are structural components of both SAGA and TFIID complexes, it is possible that TAF9B is affecting the competitive recruitment or activity of a SAGA-like complex in place of TFIID.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings.

claim: Among the genes affected by the loss of TAF9B are several targets of the Notch- and Shh-signaling pathway.
source: Among the genes affected by the loss of TAF9B are several targets of the Notch- and Shh-signaling pathway, both known to play key roles in neuronal development (reviewed by Louvi and Artavanis-Tsakonas, 2006; Jessell, 2000).
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq data analysis and supported by citations to Louvi and Artavanis-Tsakonas, 2006; Jessell, 2000.

claim: Notch- and Shh-signaling pathways are known to play key roles in neuronal development.
source: Among the genes affected by the loss of TAF9B are several targets of the Notch- and Shh-signaling pathway, both known to play key roles in neuronal development (reviewed by Louvi and Artavanis-Tsakonas, 2006; Jessell, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Louvi and Artavanis-Tsakonas, 2006; Jessell, 2000.

claim: PCAF has been shown to cooperate with p300 in Notch intracellular domain-dependent transcription assays using chromatin templates in vitro, as well as in transfection/reporter assays.
source: For example, PCAF has been shown to cooperate with another co-activator protein, p300, in Notch intracellular domain-dependent transcription assays using chromatin templates in vitro, as well as in transfection/reporter assays (Kurooka and Honjo, 2000; Wallberg et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kurooka and Honjo, 2000; Wallberg et al., 2002.

claim: Mutations in two subunits of the Drosophila DUB complex, Nonstop and Sgf11, lead to defects in neural development in the optic lobe.
source: Mutations in two subunits of the Drosophila DUB complex, Nonstop and Sgf11, lead to defects in neural development in the optic lobe (Weake et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Weake et al., 2008.

claim: In mice, mutations in the HAT domain of GCN5 result in defects in cranial neural tube closure and embryonic lethality.
source: In mice, mutations in the HAT domain of GCN5 result in defects in cranial neural tube closure and embryonic lethality (Bu et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bu et al., 2007.

claim: In humans, mutations in the DUB subunit ATXN7 are associated with the development of spinocerebellar ataxia type 7, a disease characterized by the loss of motor control as well as retinal defects.
source: In humans, mutations in the DUB subunit ATXN7 are associated with the development of spinocerebellar ataxia type 7, a disease characterized by the loss of motor control as well as retinal defects (reviewed by Koutelou et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Koutelou et al., 2010.

claim: Taf9b KO mice display defects in eye development including microphthalmia and cataracts-like phenotypes albeit with modest penetrance.
source: Interestingly, we observed that Taf9b KO mice display defects in eye development including microphthalmia and cataracts-like phenotypes albeit with modest penetrance (data not shown).
evidence: This is based on observation of the mice.

claim: The type of neuronal-specific role performed by TAF9B is reminiscent of the cell-type specific roles of particular subunits of the ATP-dependent chromatin remodeling complex BAF.
source: The type of neuronal-specific role performed by TAF9B is reminiscent of the cell-type specific roles of particular subunits of the ATP-dependent chromatin remodeling complex BAF.
evidence: This is a comparative statement drawing parallels to other known systems.

claim: The BAF complex undergoes changes in composition upon neuronal differentiation as specific BAF subunits are incorporated in neuronal progenitors cells as well as in post-mitotic neurons.
source: This complex undergoes changes in composition upon neuronal differentiation as specific BAF subunits are incorporated in neuronal progenitors cells as well as in post-mitotic neurons (Olave et al., 2002; Lessard et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Olave et al., 2002; Lessard et al., 2007.

claim: The down-regulation of neuronal genes observed in whole spinal column tissues in Taf9b KO mice may represent a specific loss of neuronal tissue relative to the surrounding vertebrae due to defects in neuronal progenitor cells during embryonic development.
source: It is also possible that the down-regulation of neuronal genes observed in whole spinal column tissues in Taf9b KO mice may represent a specific loss of neuronal tissue relative to the surrounding vertebrae due perhaps to defects in neuronal progenitor cells during embryonic development.
evidence: This is a speculative alternative explanation for the observed data.

claim: Preliminary experiments using Taf9b KO mice carrying the LacZ reporter gene suggest that Taf9b is highly expressed in the developing hypothalamus at mid-gestation.
source: Preliminary experiments using Taf9b KO mice carrying the LacZ reporter gene suggest that Taf9b is highly expressed in the developing hypothalamus at mid-gestation (data now shown).
evidence: This is based on preliminary experimental data.

claim: In a study describing neuronal activity-dependent ribosome profiling in the adult mouse hypothalamus, Taf9b can be identified as highly expressed in this tissue compared to several other TAFs.
source: In a recent study describing neuronal activity-dependent ribosome profiling in the adult mouse hypothalamus (Knight et al., 2012), Taf9b can be identified in the genomic data set as highly expressed in this tissue compared to several other TAFs.
evidence: This is based on analysis of data from Knight et al., 2012.

claim: The levels of Taf9b mRNA associated with ribosomes increased when neurons in the hypothalamus were activated, while several other TAFs were expressed at low levels or not enriched in a neuronal activity-dependent manner.
source: Moreover, the levels of Taf9b mRNA associated with ribosomes increased when neurons in the hypothalamus were activated, while several other TAFs were expressed at low levels or not enriched in a neuronal activity-dependent manner.
evidence: This is based on analysis of data from Knight et al., 2012.

claim: TAF9B may be involved in setting up transcriptional responses in at least certain neuronal circuits in the hypothalamus.
source: These results suggest that TAF9B may be involved in setting up transcriptional responses in at least certain neuronal circuits in the hypothalamus.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the ribosome profiling data.

claim: Mouse embryonic stem cells were differentiated into motor neurons using retinoic acid (RA) and the smoothened agonist SAG.
source: To examine whether the expression of various components of the core promoter recognition complex changes upon neuronal differentiation, we induced ES cells to form motor neurons using retinoic acid (RA) and the smoothened agonist SAG as described previously (Wichterle et al., 2002).
evidence: This describes the experimental method used, supported by citation to Wichterle et al., 2002.

claim: The generation of motor neurons in embryoid bodies (EBs) was confirmed by immunostaining for motor neuron-specific markers LHX3 and ISL1/2.
source: We confirmed the generation of motor neurons in embryoid bodies (EBs) by immunostaining for motor neuron-specific markers LHX3 and ISL1/2 (Figure 1A) as well as by RNA-seq analysis (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The generation of motor neurons in embryoid bodies (EBs) was confirmed by RNA-seq analysis.
source: We confirmed the generation of motor neurons in embryoid bodies (EBs) by immunostaining for motor neuron-specific markers LHX3 and ISL1/2 (Figure 1A) as well as by RNA-seq analysis (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Several TAFs are down-regulated upon motor neuron differentiation.
source: As seen in other differentiated cell types, several TAFs are down-regulated upon motor neuron differentiation (Figure 1; Deato and Tjian, 2007; D'Alessio et al., 2011; Zhou et al., 2013b; Guermah et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1 and citations to Deato and Tjian, 2007; D'Alessio et al., 2011; Zhou et al., 2013b; Guermah et al., 2003.

claim: In human HeLa cells, TAF9B had previously been reported to be a component of both the TFIID and SAGA complexes.
source: In human HeLa cells, TAF9B had previously been reported to be a component of both the TFIID and SAGA complexes (Frontini et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Frontini et al., 2005.

claim: The Taf9b KO mouse ES cells (Taf9btm1(KOMP)Vlcg) were generated by the trans-NIH Knock-Out Mouse Project (KOMP).
source: The Taf9b KO mouse ES cells (Taf9btm1(KOMP)Vlcg) were generated by the trans-NIH Knock-Out Mouse Project (KOMP) and obtained from the KOMP Repository (www.komp.org).
evidence: This describes the source of the KO cells.

claim: The Taf9b gene is located on the X chromosome.
source: Since the Taf9b gene is located in the X chromosome this male KO ES cells are a complete null for this gene.
evidence: This is stated as factual information about the gene location.
